'''''Bocconia frutescens''''' is a species of flowering plant in the [[papaveraceae|poppy family]] known by many common names, including '''plume poppy''', '''tree poppy''', '''tree celandine''', '''parrotweed''',<ref name=pier>[http://www.hear.org/pier/species/bocconia_frutescens.htm ''Bocconia frutescens.''] US Forest Service, Pacific Island Ecosystems at Risk (PIER).</ref> '''sea oxeye daisy''',<ref name=starr>Starr, F., et al. (2003). [http://www.hear.org/Pier/pdf/pohreports/bocconia_frutescens.pdf ''Bocconia frutescens''.] USGS Biological Resources Division. Haleakala Field Station, Maui, Hawai'i.</ref> and '''John Crow bush'''<ref name=chi>Chimera, C. G. 2003. [http://www.kenjinishida.net/publications/Bocconia_02Apr2002.pdf Report on ''Bocconia frutescens''.] Internal Report prepared for the Hawaii Ecosystems at Risk Project.</ref> in English, '''''gordolobo''''', '''''llorasangre''''',<ref name=san>Sánchez-Arreola, E., et al. (2006). [http://informahealthcare.com/doi/abs/10.1080/13880200600883106?journalCode=phb Alkaloids from ''Bocconia frutescens'' and biological activity of their extracts.] ''Pharmaceutical Biology'' 44(7) 540-43.</ref> '''''tabaquillo''''', '''''palo amarillo''''',<ref name=smith>[http://biogeodb.stri.si.edu/biodiversity/species/27738/ ''Bocconia frutescens''.] Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute.</ref> '''''palo de toro''''' and '''''pan cimarrón'''''<ref name=pier/> in Spanish,  '''''bois codine'''''<ref name=pier/> in French and '''''bwa kodenn ''''' in Haitian Kreyòl. It is native to the Americas, including Mexico, parts of Central and South America, and the West Indies. It is perhaps better known in [[Hawaii]], where it is an [[introduced species]] and an aggressive [[invasive species|invasive weed]] with rapid negative effects on local [[ecosystem]]s. In other parts of the United States it is used as an [[ornamental plant]] for its "tropical"-looking foliage.<ref name=chi/>

==Description==
This relative of the [[poppy]] is a [[shrub]] growing up to 6 metres tall.<ref name=starr/> It yields a bitter yellow or orange latex sap.<ref name=mot>[http://www.ctahr.hawaii.edu/invweed/WeedsHI/W_Bocconia_frutescens.pdf ''Bocconia frutescens''.] From Motooka, P., et al. (2003). ''Weeds of Hawai‘i’s Pastures and Natural Areas; An Identification and Management Guide''. College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resources, University of Hawai‘i at Manoa.</ref><ref name=hbin>[http://www.reportapest.org/pestlist/bocfru.htm Have you seen Bocconia (''Bocconia frutescens'')?] Hawaii Biodiversity Information Network.</ref> The leaves are up to 45 cm  long by 20 wide and the blades are divided into deep lobes. There are many leaves toward the ends of the branches. The [[inflorescence]] is a branching [[panicle]] up to 60 centimeters long. The purple-green flower lacks petals but has [[sepal]]s each up to a centimetre long. The [[stamen|anthers]] dangle from the flower center by their filaments. The fruit is a capsule about 1.2 cm long containing yellowish pulp and a single black seed half-sheathed in a bright red [[aril]].<ref name=starr/>

==Ecology==
This plant is capable of thriving in many types of habitat. In its native range it grows in dry, moist, and wet forests on many soil types. It is known from [[cloud forest]]s and several types of disturbed and degraded habitat. It is not, however, tolerant of dense shade.<ref name=pier/>

The seeds of the plant are generally [[seed dispersal|dispersed]] by birds, which are attracted to the pulpy fruits.<ref name=pier/><ref name=chi/> In Hawaii, the [[Japanese white-eye]] (''Zosterops japonicus'') is a common visitor to the plant. In its native range it is also an important plant for various birds.<ref name=chi/>

==Relationship with humans==
There are a number of human uses for this species, such as its use for ornamental purposes. It also has a variety of [[medicinal plant|medicinal]] uses. In Mexico it has been used to treat skin conditions and [[respiratory tract infection]]s. A laboratory study confirmed that extracts of the plant had antimicrobial action against the human pathogens ''[[Escherichia coli]]'', ''[[Staphylococcus aureus]]'', and ''[[Pseudomonas aeruginosa]]'', as well as ''[[Bacillus subtilis]]''.<ref name=san/> If the leaf is heated and applied to a wound it is said to provide pain relief. The plant can also be used as a [[dye]].<ref name=chi/>

This plant grows quickly and is a prolific producer of seeds. It was introduced to Hawaii as a garden plant around 1920, and it promptly spread to the surrounding forests and other wild habitat.<ref name=starr/> It is a problem on two of the Hawaiian islands, [[Hawaii (island)|Hawaii]] and [[Maui]]. At one spot on Hawaii it moved from the local landscaping and soon covered over 3500 acres of abandoned agricultural fields. It is a common weed of other crop fields nearby.<ref name=pier/> It easily invades [[eucalyptus]] plantations and areas of forest already dominated by non-native trees and shrubs. It is a weed of roadsides, vacant lots, and residential areas.<ref name=ben>Benitez, D. M. and D. Saulibio. (2007). [http://manoa.hawaii.edu/hpicesu/techr/144/v144.pdf ''Bocconia frutescens'' Distribution on the Island of Hawai'i.] Technical Report 144. Pacific Cooperative Studies Unit. University of Hawaii at Manoa.</ref> It is tolerant of Hawaii's [[lava]] soils.<ref name=starr/> On Maui it has been observed at [[elevation]]s near 5800 feet.<ref name=pier/> It is one of the noxious plants posing a threat to the native and rare flora of Kanaio Natural Area Reserve. The plant is thick and bushy, producing multiple stems at times and spreading densely to produce "carpets" that shade out smaller plants. Native species negatively affected include ''[[Melicope adscendens]]'', ''[[Alectryon macrococcus]]'', ''[[Bonamia menziesii]]'', ''[[Cenchrus agrimonioides]]'', ''[[Flueggea neowawraea]]'', ''[[Melicope knudsenii]]'', ''[[Santalum freycinetianum]]'' var. ''lanaiense'', and ''[[Nothocestrum latifolium]]'', a host plant of the federally endangered [[Manduca blackburni|Blackburn’s sphinx moth]] (''Manduca blackburni'').<ref name=chi/>

[[Herbicide]]s are a commonly recommended method of control for this species, particularly [[triclopyr]].<ref name=starr/><ref name=mot/> Small seedlings can be pulled by hand; larger seedlings root firmly and break if pulled, resprouting soon after. Effective control is difficult because of the plant's ability to sprout back up after being cleared off the land.<ref name=starr/> Heavy machinery should be cleaned after digging in infested areas to prevent the transfer of seeds. Aerial monitoring of vulnerable areas is also recommended.<ref name=ben/>
